 The Fall Skin Care Reset: What to Change in Your Routine Now 
 The Fall Skin Care Reset: What to Change in Your Routine Now 
 Cooler temps call for richer textures, smarter exfoliation, and a stronger focus on barrier support.
 By Nykia Spradley Published: Oct 21, 2026 Save Article Share Article Artem Varnitsin // Getty Images Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy. 
 The jackets are out, the boots are broken in, and your skin may already feel far gone from its dewy, summer best. All signs point to fall being in full swing, and it’s time to transition your skincare routine to focus on hydration, exfoliation, and barrier support. You may not need to push the creams and serums you’ve been using to the back of your cabinet, but your skin care lineup will likely benefit from a few added ingredients. Experts share how to reset your skin care routine for fall to get ahead of the dry, cold days ahead.
 What happens to skin in the fall?
 As we transition into fall, Dr . Aya Ahram , a board-certified dermatologist at Hudson Dermatology and Laser Surgery , says we lose some of the moisture in the air and ultimately our skin. “The biggest change I recommend is shifting the focus from lightweight products to a routine that prioritizes hydration and barrier support,” she tells ELLE. Cooler temperatures and lower humidity can increase water loss in the skin, leaving skin feeling tight, flaky, or irritated. Pay attention to your lips, hands, and body as well. These areas, Ahram says, are often overlooked until they become dry or cracked.
 Seasonal changes can affect everyone, but Ahram notes that the way the skin responds varies depending on a person’s baseline skin type, skin barrier, and any underlying skin conditions. For those with dry and sensitive skin, she says you may notice tightness, flaking, redness, and stinging as humidity decreases. “Patients with eczema or rosacea may also experience more frequent flares and should prioritize gentle cleansing and barrier repair. If you have more oily skin, you still should moisturize your skin, although you might be able to get by with a water-based gel cream rather than a thicker cream,” Ahram adds.
 What are the must-have products in a fall skin routine?
 Starting with your cleanser, Ahram suggests switching from a foaming cleanser to a gentler, hydrating formula that doesn’t strip the skin of its natural moisturizing factors. And since moisture will be the hero of your lineup in these colder months, Ahram also recommends looking for moisture-attracting and sealing ingredients such as ceramides, glycerin, hyaluronic acid, and petrolatum, depending on your skin type. Rachel Liverman, aesthetician and Glowbar founder and CEO, recommends adding a hydrating serum and swapping to a richer moisturizer to help support your skin barrier.
 For those often-forgotten extremities, Ahram says a richer hand cream and a lip ointment like Aquaphor or Vaseline can help prevent irritation before it starts.
 Both experts say that although the scorching sunny days of summer are behind us, sunscreen is a non-negotiable, even in the fall. “Continue wearing sunscreen daily, since UVA rays contribute to photoaging and pigmentation year-round, and incidental sun exposure still adds up,” says Ahram.
 What professional and at-home treatments best complement each other in the fall? 
 Liverman says that as dry skin creeps in, it’s also a great time of year to pair professional exfoliation, like a Glowbar facial , with a consistent at-home routine. “In-office treatments like dermaplaning and chemical peels help resurface the skin, while at-home chemical exfoliants can help maintain those results between treatments. Don't overdo it either; the key to healthy skin is balance,” Liverman says. The cooler weather makes deeper exfoliation more tolerable for skin since the lower sun exposure makes it easier for your skin to recover and reset. “It's also an ideal time to address buildup and dullness from summer months, but again, balance is key,” Liverman adds.
 Additionally, Ahram adds that since skin will be less exposed to damaging sun rays, in-office treatments and incorporating a retinol are ideal in the fall—as long as it is well tolerated to help with texture, hyperpigmentation, and antiaging. “It is something that can be done consistently and can help maintain results from laser,” Ahram explains. “Fall is also a great time to start incorporating procedures such as lasers or microneedling to help with gentle resurfacing, pigmentation, collagen-building, texture, and glow,” she adds. What’s important, though, is that the professional treatments and home care you choose should complement one another. “I generally recommend avoiding excessive exfoliation and carefully coordinating retinoids, acids, and procedures to minimize irritation,” says Ahram.
 What ingredient should you add to your routine right now?
 If your core lineup is set and you’re looking to add one ingredient to keep your skin in check until spring, Liverman says to make it a retinol. “Fall has less intense sun exposure than in the summer, so your skin has more time to adjust to retinol and build tolerance. It can be drying and irritating at first, so you want to start slowly—and pair it with plenty of hydration,” Liverman notes. Retinol, as well as other chemical exfoliants, is a great addition during winter when sun exposure is at a minimum. She suggests starting one or two times a week, while incorporating hydrating products to maintain your skin barrier.
 Ahram agrees, adding that retinoids are among the best-studied topical ingredients for acne, uneven skin tone, and photoaging. “They help increase skin cell turnover and can improve the appearance of fine lines and skin texture over time,” Ahram says.
 Although retinoids are beneficial for addressing accumulated sun damage, uneven tone, or breakouts, Ahram says that if you’re experiencing dryness, sensitivity, or inflammation, prioritize barrier-supporting ingredients first. “Ceramides are lipids that help maintain the skin’s protective barrier,” she notes, adding that they also help reduce dryness and irritation. Ceramides are commonly found in most moisturizers. Glycerin and hyaluronic acid, humectants that attract and retain water in the skin, are also barrier-supporting ingredients that Ahram highly recommends adding in, too—not only for the moisture retention, but to help improve the appearance of dehydration-related fine lines.
 What should you avoid as the season changes?
 Liverman says to avoid making too many major changes to your routine at once. “If you’re introducing stronger products or actives, like retinol or chemical exfoliants, add them in slowly. Overdoing it can overwhelm your skin and lead to dryness and irritation, especially as the weather gets colder,” she warns.
 Ahram shares a similar sentiment, noting that with so many products available, it is easy to want to introduce retinol, exfoliating acids, new cleansers, and professional treatments simultaneously, only to end up with an irritated skin barrier. “A complicated routine isn’t necessarily a better routine. A gentle cleanser, an appropriate moisturizer, sunscreen, and one well-chosen active ingredient can be more effective than a shelf full of products,” says Ahram. If you are adding new products to your routine, try to avoid overlapping the actives. “Introduce one new product at a time so that you can assess tolerance and identify the cause if irritation develops. It's important to pay attention to your skin as the season changes and new products are being incorporated. Persistent burning, stinging, redness, and scaling are not signs that a product is working better,” says Ahram.
 You’ll also want to avoid over-exfoliation. “Try not to combine multiple exfoliating products or use scrubs on skin that is already dry or peeling. The peeling is usually a sign that you need more hydration in your skin, not exfoliation,” Ahram points out.
 Lastly, and this is one you’ve likely heard often: don’t turn up the water temperature. “As the weather gets cooler, it's tempting to want to take long, hot showers, which can worsen dryness. Shorter showers with warm water, followed by immediate moisturizing, are preferable,” Ahram concludes.
